Bng. chō ‘call for driving away dogs’, Deog. chō-chō ‘call for prompting dogs to chase after game’ — Pr. sösöli- etc. ‘to bait (with dogs); hetzen (Hund)’ — also borrowed into New. cyai cyai ‘the sound used in calling a dog meaning to chase somebody’ — also borrowed into Dravidian, see DEDR 2718: cū ‘sound uttered in setting on dogs’ and Brah. čuh ‘call to a dog’ — cf. perhaps Bon. gu-soʔ, soʔ ‘dog’ — PMK *cɔʔ ‘dog’, Tampuan choo ‘dog’, Chong cʰoː ‘dog’, Semelai cɔːh ‘dog’, Proto-Bahnaric *cɔː ‘dog’ and Stieng chɔː ‘dog’, Kui chɛ̤ːʔ ‘word used to chase dogs away’, Khasi ʃuː ‘to set a dog upon’, Proto-Khmuic *cɔʔ ‘dog’ and Mlabri chɔɔʔ ‘dog’, Bolyu ʦu⁵³hu¹³ ‘hunting dog’, Nyah Kur chéʔ-chéʔ ‘sound of chasing a dog away’, Proto-Palaungic *cɔʔ ‘dog’, Proto-Pearic *c(ɔ)ʔ ‘dog’, Proto-Pong *cɔː³ ‘chien, dog’ and Vietnamese (Hanoi) chó ‘dog’, etc. Notes: (a) There cannot be any doubt that the lemma is of Austro-Asiatic origin. How- ever, showing very few, if any, reflexes in Munda and being borrowed also into Tibeto-Himalayan and Dravidian indicates that the borrowings must have oc- curred very early, perhaps before the arrival of the ancestors of the Munda lan- guages. It seems also likely that the lemma designated especially a hunting dog. (b) Despite somewhat different semantics, here probably also Ind. čhòʰ ‘a call for driving away cattle’, Bur./Sh. ćho ‘away! (to cows)’ and K. chuh ‘noise made in driving a horse’.

The following lemmata (a) and (b) are possibly etymologically related, though this is not totally clear: (a) Bng. ḍɔrḍɔrɔ ‘bumpy and stony (slope)’, Rp. ḍāṭ pūv ‘footbridge made of stone’ (second word ← Pers. pul), Garh. ḍaul ‘stony area in the mountains’ — Ind. ḍáḍʌr ‘a scree’, Kal. ḍaró ‘rocky or stony place’, Bur./Sh.  ḍáḍar ‘scree’ and probably Bur.ys. ḍanḍákhal ‘stony’, Sh.gur. ḍīḍ b- ‘to slip and fall’, Ḍ. ḍʌḍəra ‘scree’, Pal. aḍar-kóḍur ‘bumpy (ground)’ (Strand), ḍuḍurū-m ‘to roll, fall’ and baṭṭa duḍurila “falling stones”? (Morgenstierne [1941a: 34] here describes this too briefly; it is possible that the initial dental stop in his duḍurila is a printing mistake; however, cf. also Khot. dädäya- ‘boul- der’ and there is also Pal. dhiaáṛ ‘pieces of rock, collection of stones in one place’, and see below note [i]) — Mult. ḍoḍar kã̄ ‘a raven; a mountain crow’ — Brah. ḍal ‘gravelly ground along the skirt of a hill’. Cf. also Psht. ḍabara ‘pebble, stone, boulder’ (with dissimilation of stops?) and Pr. ḍugur ‘rock’ (perhaps a synonym compound with second syllable < OIA girí- ‘rock, mountain’) — it appears quite impossible to deny etymological connection with Proto-Kherwarian *d(h)iri ‘rock, stone’ and its many reflexes in modern Munda languages (note especially Sant. dhiri ∼ dihri ‘rock, stone’ with ‘phoneme split’). The lemma seems to have no MK parallels (see Pinnow 84) and thus is apparently a ‘North Indian’ word. (b) Bng. ḍaḍɔ n.m. ‘projection or protrusion on a mountainside, a steep and high slope; heights’, Deog. ḍāḍɔ ‘steep rocks high up on a mountain’, Rudh. ḍaḍḍəl ‘precipice’, Old Cam. ḍhaḍhā, ḍāḍ, ḍāḍara ‘precipice’ — Ind. ḍʌ̀ḍ ‘alpine pasture’, Wg. ḍaḍə ‘steep hillside’ — Sant. daɽaŋ ‘a slope, steep embankment; steep, precipitous’ and daɽaŋ daɽaŋ ‘very steep, precipitous’ and dãːɽga, daːɽŋga ‘precipice, steep slope; precipitous embankment; steep, precipitous’ (also Deśi dāṛṅga), dhaɽ dhaɽ ‘steep’ and dhaɽ dhạɽiạ ‘steep, precipitous, up and down’. Notes: (i) The Sant. forms sub (b) with initial dental stop must be older and phonolog- ically closer to the original ‘North Indian’ lemma than the quoted IA forms with initial retroflex stop which must be later borrowings that also underwent CCH. (ii)The above words need to be kept separate from the following similar sound- ing Bng. words: ḍaḍṇɔ ‘to shove food into o.s. (e.g. during the feast of freshly slaughtered animals in the month of Māgh); to fill sausages with fresh meat’ with the first meaning < OIA *ḍaḍḍha-² ‘belly’ (5575) and the second meaning < OIA *ḍaḍḍha-¹ ‘fat, swollen’ (5575); in the case of the next two words it is not quite clear whether only OIA 5575 is the origin or even OIA *ḍaḍḍha-³ ‘drum’ (5576): ḍàḍi n.m. ‘a professional low-caste musician who does not follow the travels of his deity (as most others do) but who ‘belongs’ to a Rajput’ (cf. OP. and P. ḍhāḍhī ‘bard, minstrel’ and Pr. ḍaḍ ‘two-sided drum’); ḍè̄ḍ ‘an abusive term against Koḷis (basically meaning ‘outcast’)’ which cf. with Rj.jaip. ḍheḍh ‘a contemptuous term for a weaver and a tanner’.

Wilderness: hill, mountain; forest (a) Indo-Aryan, Iranian, West Himalayish and Tibeto-Burman: Bng. ruṅgi dà̄r and Deog. rugi dhār ‘a mountain range above the treeline’ (second element <OIA dhá̄rā- ‘edge of mountain’ [6793]) — Ind. rugí̄ ‘alpine pasture’, Bur./Sh. ruṅ ‘upland pasture, pasture ground on hills’, Sh. and Pal. rugṛī ‘ditto’, Bro. ruṅ ‘hill; forest’ — Wkh. c̣uk rag ‘a ridge (vertical)’ (Yoshie) — Bun. rwaṅ ‘mountain pasture’, Kann. răṅ ‘hill, mountain’ (Bailey) (cf. also Kann. roṅmiʔg ‘to graze’), Pur. ruṅ ‘mountain pass’ and probably Paṭṭ. rəṅgi ‘high; height’, Lāh. raṅ ‘hill’ and raṅgi ‘high’, and perhaps Chit. rāk ‘alpine meadow’ (Z.); Zz. rang, rvang ‘mountain’ — rGyalrong (spoken in Sichuan) ˈrəngu ‘mountain’ (STEDT). Note: Matisoff observes (2001: 10) on Zz. raṅ and Kinn. raṅtsō both ‘moun- tain’: “Many other TB languages of Nepal and NE India have cognates with liquid initials, most with l-: Chepang sy-a-a-lung, Mikir ing-long, Khoirao a-long, Rongmei long-kau, Liangmei lwang-ku; but one Kamarupan language has r: Maram rawong. Sulong and Lushai (Mizo) both provide evidence for a velar prefix: Sulong gɹaṅ, Lushai tlâng (Lu. tl- regularly <*gl-, thl- <*kl-). We may reconstruct PTB *g-l/r(w)aṅ.” Matisoff’s reconstruction is similar with the STEDT reconstruction for PKC *klaaṅ ‘hill; mountain’ (provisional) which, in turn, cf. with AA Bahnar kooŋ ‘mountain, high hill’ and Halang kraːŋ ‘mountain; cliff’. (b) Munda: So. kən(d)ˈreːŋ-ən ‘forest’ (with kən(d)- clearly originally meaning ‘for- est’ ) and ˈboːŋ-ən a forest, hill’ probably < *buru-roŋ or a similarly built compound because of Bodo-Gadaba buroŋ ‘hill, mountain’, Ho. maˈraːŋ bu r̩u ‘mountain’ (first word compares with Proto-Waic *mloŋ ‘mountain’); cf. also Bon. siloŋ ‘hill’ which looks similar like Proto-Monic *slooŋ ‘the top part of, e.g. a mountain, clouds, sky’ and with TB Chepang sy-a-a-lung ‘mountain’. (c) Mon-Khmer: Among the following examples there may be contamination of PMK *ruuŋ[ ], *ruŋʔ, *ruəŋ all ‘ridge, spine, back’ and PMK *ru(u)k ‘forest’: Riang raṅ ‘hill, mountain’, Ngeq rɔŋ ‘forest’ and Pacoh rɯːŋ ‘forest’, Khmer rɔ̀ːŋ ‘ridge for plant- ing crops’, Car ɾuŋ ‘hill, ridge, crest’ and ɾɔːŋə ‘the back bone, thick ridge (or spine) of the plantain leaf; a mountain chain, hill’, Maleng (Bro) rɔŋʔ ‘back, ridge’, Khmu reːŋ ‘forest that was used as field’ and rŋkɔːŋ ‘ridge, mountain range’ (which looks like a compound *reːŋ-kɔːŋ) and Phong ʔərəːŋ ‘forest’ (cf. Khoirao a-long ‘mountain’), Riang _raŋ ‘hill, mountain’ and Wa brạ̄ng ‘mountain’, mːlong and lang ‘mountain’, and Lawa mblaoŋ ‘mountain’ and Samtau mkọṅ ‘mountain’ (second part of last word connected with Bahnar kooŋ) and Riang cɔkɨ raŋ² ‘mountain top’, Proto-Vietic *k-rəŋ ‘forest’ (PKC *klaaṅ ‘hill; mountain’). Note: Mult. “rugg” and P. rug ‘sandy uncultivated land; sandy soil’ (O’Brien) and P. rã̄g ‘a great mountain ridge’, Oss. rāɣ ‘back, ridge’, Psht. rāɣˈə ‘skirt of a mountain’, Brah. ruṅg ‘hill-track; short cut’, Bal. raɣ ‘mountain ridge’ and Bal. rūṅgrā and Jaṭ. ruṅg rāh ‘hill-track; short cut’ (the semantic modification is due to the suffixation with Pers. rāh) seem to be influenced by or connected with Pers. rāɣ ‘land at the foot of a mountain, mountainside’.

text: 474 This semantic interlocking is not far-fetched. Cf. e.g. p. 593 the word for ‘woman’ in quite many West Pahāṛī varieties, which reflects OIA *chedu- ‘cut, slit’ (5067b). The otherwise usual word for ‘copulate’ is leċṇɔ < *licca- ‘defective’ (11053) which has a semantic parallel in Brah. liččikī ‘copulation of dogs’ and which may have an Austro-Asiatic etymological background, see PMK *lɔ(ɔ)c ‘penis’ with many modern reflexes.
